nodes.summary: Ten days later every page carries a pane whose model is given seven tools that run in the page over an index the build emits, and the pane shows every call it made.

nodes.label: One site's copy, not a versioned module
nodes.summary: The site-wide pane is still one site's copy rather than a versioned module the other eighteen sites can load, and that row decides whether this was worth doing.

nodes.label: Routing, not teaching
nodes.summary: The panel points you at a site rather than answering questions about the subjects, because a summary that drifts from the arguments is worse than a link that does not.

quotes.text: The important property: a reader should never have to hold a credential to use an index.
quotes.why: The rule that makes the free local matcher the default rather than the model.

quotes.text: A chat box on one site is a feature. The same panel on all nineteen, reading each site's own catalogue, is the thing that makes a network of nineteen sites navigable, and it is why the catalogue is generated rather than written.
quotes.why: Why the piece is about a network's navigation rather than one widget.

articles.title: Twenty sites in fifteen days, and what that did to the writing
articles.teaser: One site became twenty repositories in fifteen days because each argument needed its own version history, and the index now starts from a question.

graph.teaser: One site became twenty repositories in fifteen days because each argument needed its own version history, and the index now starts from a question.
graph.core_idea: A body of work outgrew the site it was published in and split into nineteen siblings so each argument could keep its own version history, and the index into them starts from the reader's question rather than a list of names.

nodes.label: Twenty repositories in fifteen days
nodes.summary: On 11 August this was one website; by 26 August there were twenty repositories, nineteen of them siblings on *.sgit.ai, fifteen created in the last five days.

nodes.label: A section is a promise
nodes.summary: A section promises that something is part of the thing it sits inside, and that promise stopped holding when the writing answered questions that were not about sgit.

nodes.label: Its own version history
nodes.summary: Nineteen arguments moving at different speeds through one release log produces a record nobody can read; split, each gets its own record of when it changed its mind.

nodes.label: Discovery got worse
nodes.summary: Nineteen domains is not a menu; names like nfrs.sgit.ai and issues-fs.sgit.ai mean nothing until you already know what they argue.

nodes.label: Consistency by discipline
nodes.summary: One site has one stylesheet by construction; nineteen have one stylesheet by discipline, and discipline is the thing that quietly stops happening.

nodes.label: Cross-link drift
nodes.summary: The audit found graphs.sgit.ai pointing at sentinel.sgit.ai, which does not exist; the site is sg-sentinel.sgit.ai, one character of drift and the link is dead.

nodes.label: Start from the question
nodes.summary: The directory starts from the question the reader arrived with, seventeen lines of it, then five groups by area, then a table of all nineteen.

nodes.label: Every thesis in the site's own words
nodes.summary: Each thesis on the directory page is quoted from the site's H1 or lede rather than summarised, because a summary drifts and a quotation either matches or is visibly wrong.

nodes.label: Same generator, same release script
nodes.summary: Same generator, same stylesheet, same release script, same validator, same rule that publishing is adding one file.

nodes.label: Publishing is adding one file
nodes.summary: Adding the twentieth site is writing one markdown file, the same property that lets two agents publish on the same day without conflict.

nodes.label: skills.sgit.ai, not published yet
nodes.summary: One of the nineteen has a repository and a DNS record and nothing behind it, listed as not published yet rather than quietly omitted.

nodes.label: Arguments, not products
nodes.summary: sg-sentinel says NOT BUILT, risks states zero lines of code implement its model, wardley-maps is PROPOSED: publish the argument before the thing exists and say what it is worth.

quotes.text: A summary drifts. A quotation either matches or is visibly wrong.
quotes.why: The rule that keeps the directory honest, and the reason the index quotes each site rather than describing it.

quotes.text: One character of drift, and the link is dead.
quotes.why: The concrete cost of splitting: a link between sites is a claim about another site that has to be checked.

articles.title: Git for things you cannot put on GitHub
articles.teaser: sgit is git for files you cannot put on GitHub: encrypted before they leave your machine, versioned like git, stored where the server cannot read a byte.

graph.teaser: sgit is git for files you cannot put on GitHub: encrypted before they leave your machine, versioned like git, stored where the server cannot read a byte.
graph.core_idea: sgit gives the files people say they cannot put on GitHub the history, branches and shareable links of git, on a server that holds ciphertext and nothing else.

nodes.label: Files with nowhere good to live
nodes.summary: A risk register with real system names, a regulatory analysis still being argued about, the working memory of an AI agent, client material under NDA.

nodes.label: sgit
nodes.summary: sgit is git for those files: encrypted before they leave your machine, versioned exactly like git, stored on a server that cannot read a single byte.

nodes.label: Zero knowledge, precisely
nodes.summary: The server holds ciphertext and nothing else, not your filenames, not your directory structure, not your commit messages.

nodes.label: No key escrow
nodes.summary: There is no key escrow, no admin override, no support engineer who can recover it for you, and that last part is a feature with a real cost.

nodes.label: Vault key
nodes.summary: A single string that is three things at once, the address of the vault, the authorisation to write to it, and the key that decrypts it.

nodes.label: Read key
nodes.summary: Derived one way from the vault key, same vault, read-only, safe to publish, and that asymmetry is the whole sharing model.

nodes.label: Release tripwire
nodes.summary: No vault key has ever been published, a rule enforced by a tripwire in the release pipeline that scans every file before either remote is touched.

nodes.label: Content-addressed over ciphertext
nodes.summary: The object's name is a SHA-256 of the encrypted bytes, so the host can deduplicate it, cache it and serve it from a CDN while unable to tell you what it is.

nodes.label: A real version control system
nodes.summary: Multi-parent commits, a tree per directory, deterministic refs derived by HMAC, a genuine merge-base computation and three-way merge, on content the server cannot interpret.

nodes.label: Nineteen vaults you can open
nodes.summary: Every vault on sgit.ai is live, and cloning all nineteen from their published keys gave 1,389 files and no failures.

nodes.label: Capability without credential
nodes.summary: A vault can contain an application that requests no permissions and still renders the whole risk graph, because the host reads the vault and passes results in.

nodes.label: The network of sites
nodes.summary: sgit.ai is one of nineteen sites on *.sgit.ai, each taking one question further than a section could.

nodes.label: Checkable rather than impressive
nodes.summary: Each site publishes its argument before the thing exists and states plainly what has shipped and what has not.

quotes.text: Lose it and the data is gone. Leak it and someone can rewrite your history.
quotes.why: The two costs of a vault key being address, authorisation and encryption key at once.

quotes.text: We would rather be checkable than impressive.
quotes.why: The house style that the live vaults, the version log and the NOT BUILT pages all follow.

articles.title: Seven vaults, one method
articles.teaser: Publishing seven encrypted vaults in a fortnight produced a method, and every rule in it exists because something went wrong first.

graph.teaser: Publishing seven encrypted vaults in a fortnight produced a method, and every rule in it exists because something went wrong first.
graph.core_idea: A repeatable method for publishing encrypted vaults, each rule learned by getting something wrong first, starting with classifying the credential before it touches anything.

nodes.label: Classify the credential
nodes.summary: Classify the credential before it touches anything, because three of the seven vaults arrived as a vault key described as a read key.

nodes.label: Vault key
nodes.summary: A vault key is write access, and because it is also the address and the encryption root there is no revocation, no rotation, and no undo.

nodes.label: Read key
nodes.summary: A read key is 64 hex characters, derived one-way from a vault key, and safe to publish.

nodes.label: check_credential.py
nodes.summary: A script that classifies a credential by shape, exits 0 for publishable and 1 for stop, and never echoes what it was given.

nodes.label: Release validator tripwire
nodes.summary: The release validator scans every tracked file for any key-shaped string and for the actual passphrases, and has caught its own author three times.

nodes.label: Derive rather than refuse
nodes.summary: A submission that cannot be published can still become one that can, by deriving the read key and putting the vault key in a gitignored tier.

nodes.label: Strictly less capability
nodes.summary: The whole shape of the project is a capability you can hand over that is strictly less than the one you hold, with the reduction enforced by mathematics rather than by policy.

nodes.label: Audit with the key you publish
nodes.summary: Audit every file with exactly the credential a reader will have, not with the vault key.

nodes.label: Sealed LLM credential check
nodes.summary: One vault carried a sealed LLM credential, and attempting to open it with the published read key got InvalidTag from AES-GCM, so no budget was exposed.

nodes.label: Risk Graph Explorer
nodes.summary: The sixth vault was public by design, with its own PUBLIC.md whose third rule, no metered capability behind a published read key, was adopted into the guidance.

nodes.label: Capture evidence by driving the real product
nodes.summary: Every screenshot is taken by opening the actual vault in a real browser with the published read key, and the rig grew an appProbe step to ask the app what its elements are called.

nodes.label: Describe, show, then admit
nodes.summary: Every vault page ends with what the vault does not do, as a section with the same weight as the features.

nodes.label: Publishing playbook
nodes.summary: The method is written down as a playbook aimed at another site's agent rather than at us, which was the real test of whether it was a method or just a habit.

nodes.label: The honest ledger
nodes.summary: Three vault keys caught, one budget exposure checked and cleared, one upstream rule adopted, and three bugs found by testing rather than assumption.

quotes.text: Which is the point: a rule that only catches other people is not a rule.
quotes.why: The tripwire catching its own author is what turns a habit into a control.

quotes.text: A published vault is an argument that this way of working is sound; an argument that omits its own edges is a brochure.
quotes.why: The reason every vault page ends with what the vault does not do.

articles.title: Green does not mean live
articles.teaser: Two releases passed every check and never reached the site because the checks stopped at the git remote; a release now ends by asking the live site its version.

graph.teaser: Two releases passed every check and never reached the site because the checks stopped at the git remote; a release now ends by asking the live site its version.
graph.core_idea: Shipped is a fact about the reader, not about your repository, so a release has to verify the boundary the reader is on and not only the ones the repository can see.

nodes.label: Two releases that never reached anybody
nodes.summary: Two consecutive releases pushed cleanly, printed both remotes in sync, and the site served a two-release-old page for forty minutes until a human on a phone asked if it was the latest version.

nodes.label: The version badge
nodes.summary: The badge on the home page that a human looked at to notice the miss, and that the release now polls for the new version.

nodes.label: Checking the wrong boundary
nodes.summary: The checks were not weak; they were checking the wrong boundary.

nodes.label: What the release actually verified
nodes.summary: Build the site, run the validator, commit and push the encrypted vault and confirm sync, commit and push the git mirror and confirm HEAD equals origin/dev.

nodes.label: The bytes arrived at GitHub
nodes.summary: HEAD == origin/dev compares hashes, not hopes, but it means the bytes arrived at GitHub, not that anybody can read them.

nodes.label: Three boundaries, two verified
nodes.summary: Source to git remote, git remote to Pages deploy, Pages deploy to the reader; a GitHub Actions job sits in the unverified gap and reports into a system neither remote knows about.

nodes.label: What actually failed
nodes.summary: The deploy job died in Set up job because codeload.github.com rate-limited the download of actions/configure-pages with a 429, while the validate and tag-release jobs passed.

nodes.label: The most likely thing to break is not your code
nodes.summary: It is a piece of shared infrastructure you do not run, on a day you were not thinking about it.

nodes.label: Ask the live site what version it is serving
nodes.summary: A release now polls sgit.ai with a cache-buster for the new version, up to eight minutes, and aborts loudly if it never appears, naming the Actions page.

nodes.label: Shipped is a fact about the reader
nodes.summary: Shipped is a fact about the reader, not about your repository.

nodes.label: Three rules of the same shape
nodes.summary: A page nothing links to, a page the machine index omits, and a page the deploy never served are all unpublished, and the build or the release fails on each.

nodes.label: What this does not fix
nodes.summary: It detects a failed deploy but does not repair one, it checks only the home page's badge so a partial deploy would pass, and it adds up to eight minutes to every release.

quotes.text: The checks were not weak. They were checking the wrong boundary.
quotes.why: The diagnosis: strong checks on the wrong side of the deploy.

quotes.text: All three are the same claim: shipped is a fact about the reader, not about your repository.
quotes.why: The general rule the fix joins, learned from three failures of the same shape.
